content:
Reported latest iOS 27 beta camera app code suggests major pro photo and video features incoming.

While the stock Camera app has steadily gained features over time, the discoveries are still surprising for an app primarily designed for point-and-shoot photography…

Apple has historically tried to strike a balance between making its own Camera app incredibly easy to use for snapshot purposes, while also offering some degree of creative control for users who like to use it as a professional camera. However, despite the app's gradual evolution, most serious photographers and videographers still prefer to use third-party apps.

If the discoveries are accurate, some of the powerful features reportedly being introduced—typically found only on professional cameras—could very well change that. Developer pdfu says the code they found supports four major features that are not currently enabled in any beta.

Exposure Range Tools

Judging exposure by sight alone is unreliable, especially when looking at the iPhone screen in bright sunlight. Most professional cameras support a histogram feature that accurately shows exposure status, while video editing software tends to use a waveform as another way to display the same information. Pdfu says they found code for both of these features inside the beta.

Focus Peaking

How much of a photo, from the nearest foreground to the farthest background, is in focus depends on several factors, but in some scenes only part of the range will be sharp. Focus range is likewise difficult to judge accurately by eye alone, which is why professional-grade camcorders specifically employ a technique called focus peaking.

When enabled, an overlay is added that highlights the in-focus parts of the image, usually in red—though the example on the left uses yellow.

Highlight Overexposure Warning

The biggest risk with exposure errors is over-exposure. Generally speaking, if you under-expose the shadow areas, you can usually save it in post—unless it's severely off, shadows rarely end up completely black (RGB values of zero). Over-exposure is much more problematic because it can easily blow out the highlights entirely—meaning the bright areas exceed RGB value 255 and cannot be recovered in post.

Many professional cameras use an indicator called zebra stripes that marks blown-out areas with red diagonal lines. Some models also let you manually set the threshold for this warning so you can be alerted as you approach—for example, at 90%—rather than only after you've already blown out the highlights.

This feature is also shown in the top right image above.

Manual Focus

The Camera app currently lets you lock focus on a subject in the frame, but it must be used in conjunction with AE/AF Lock (Auto Exposure / Auto Focus) in order to also lock exposure at that same point.

The report says Apple has been testing the addition of true manual focus via a slider in the Camera app. According to Pdfu, this feature may be limited to one or more upcoming new iPhones.

Other Features

Beyond the professional features, a burst-mode countdown photo option is reportedly also being added. When taking group photos, many people often want to take multiple shots, so this feature makes it easy to set your iPhone on a tripod or place it in a suitable position, then snap a series of photos in a row and pick one that everyone is happy with.

Finally, there are indications that a new image processing method will be adopted to accommodate the variable aperture design expected on the iPhone 18 Pro.

9to5Mac's Take

None of the features above are enabled in any iOS 27 beta, and I would be surprised if Apple actually puts these things in the stock Camera app rather than restricting them to Final Cut Camera. Still, the report does seem to carry some credibility.

What do you think of this report? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
